prompt: In this repository, the addDependency function throws "A task cannot depend on itself" whenever it's called with the same task id for both its task_id and depends_on_task_id arguments. One of addDependency's callers builds a whole batch of new tasks from a single client-supplied list of task specs, where each spec may carry its own temporary client-chosen id and a depends_on list of references — each reference resolving either to another spec in the same batch (by that spec's temporary id) or to an already-existing task id. Trace forward from that batch-creating caller and explain precisely what shape of client input triggers addDependency's self-dependency error through this path, even though no single spec in the batch ever literally repeats its own real task id as its own dependency. Name the function where this happens, and describe the exact input shape that triggers the bug.

oracle.rubric: The question: which caller of addDependency (src/domain/dependencies.ts) can trigger its 'A task cannot depend on itself' self-dependency error even though no single input spec literally repeats its own real task id as its own dependency value. Ground truth, confirmed by reading src/domain/tasks.ts's createTasks function (the domain function behind the create_tasks MCP tool): createTasks first creates every task in the batch, populating a temp_id -> real task_id map; it then walks each spec's depends_on list a second time, resolving each entry through that map (falling back to treating it as a literal existing task_id if it isn't a known temp_id). If a spec supplies its own temp_id inside its own depends_on array (e.g. {temp_id: 'a', depends_on: ['a']}), that reference resolves back to the same task's own just-created id, so addDependency ends up called with the same id for both arguments and throws the self-dependency error — even though the raw input JSON never repeats a literal real task id anywhere. PASS only if the answer (a) names createTasks (or unambiguously identifies the create_tasks batch-creation function/tool) as the caller responsible, AND (b) describes the triggering condition as a spec whose depends_on list references its own temp_id (or an equivalent precise description of a spec depending on itself via its own client-chosen temporary id, resolved only after all tasks in the batch are created). FAIL if the answer blames a different function (e.g. the direct add_dependency tool, or splitTask) as the root cause of this specific self-triggering bug, if it fails to identify the temp_id self-reference mechanism (e.g. only vaguely says 'bad input' without identifying the temp_id resolution step), or if it claims this scenario cannot happen / no such bug exists. Wording, the exact input JSON shown, and additional correct detail do not matter.

prompt: Product wants a 'bulk-close-out' operation for epics: when an epic is abandoned, mark every one of its tasks that isn't already done or cancelled as cancelled, in one call. Investigate this codebase and describe exactly how you'd implement it — which existing function handles cancelling a single task (and what it already guards against), how you'd get the list of tasks in an epic, and what has to be handled correctly so the bulk operation doesn't just crash on the first already-finished task or blow up on a task someone else is actively working on.

oracle.rubric: The question: how would you implement a bulk-cancel-all-open-tasks-in-an-epic operation in this codebase. Ground truth, confirmed by reading the actual code: (1) src/domain/lifecycle.ts's cancelTask function is the existing single-task primitive whose behavior/guards the plan must build on rather than inventing unrelated logic — it already throws if the task's status is 'done' or 'cancelled', and checks owner_session_id/lock_expires_at unless a force flag is passed. A correct plan may either call cancelTask directly per task (handling the exceptions it throws), or explicitly propose sharing/extracting its existing checks into a shared helper so both cancelTask and the new bulk operation use the same logic without cancelTask's own exceptions as loop control flow — both are valid engineering choices; what fails is a plan that ignores cancelTask's existing guards entirely and reinvents unrelated ad hoc cancellation logic from scratch. (2) Listing a specific epic's tasks already has a precedent in src/domain/status.ts: epicTaskCounts/getEpicStatus queries `SELECT id, status FROM tasks WHERE epic_id = ?` — the correct answer should point at this epic_id-scoped query shape (or getEpicStatus/listEpicsWithStatus), not invent an unrelated way to enumerate an epic's tasks. (3) Because cancelTask throws on a task that is already done/cancelled, a bulk operation that just loops and calls cancelTask on every task in the epic would crash on the first already-finished one — the answer must explicitly say to filter out done/cancelled tasks before calling cancelTask (or otherwise skip/catch that case per task) rather than assuming a bare loop works. (4) The answer must also address that a task currently claimed/locked by another session will make cancelTask throw a conflict error unless force is passed, and say something concrete about that (e.g. pass force, or skip locked tasks, or surface the conflict) rather than ignoring it entirely. PASS only if the answer's plan (a) demonstrably builds on cancelTask's existing guards (by calling it directly or by sharing/extracting its logic) rather than ignoring it and reinventing unrelated cancellation logic, (b) correctly describes getting an epic's tasks via the epic_id-scoped query/status-domain functions, (c) explicitly handles skipping already-done/cancelled tasks before calling cancelTask, and (d) explicitly addresses the locked/claimed-task case. FAIL if the plan ignores cancelTask's existing guards entirely and reinvents unrelated cancellation logic, invents a wrong way to enumerate an epic's tasks (e.g. searching all tasks with no epic filter), omits handling already-done/cancelled tasks (i.e. describes a bare loop that would crash), or never mentions the locked-task/force case at all. Wording, exact function names for a brand-new bulk function, and additional correct detail do not matter.
